In React, what's the core difference between props and state?
fields.Back: Props are read-only data passed from a parent to configure a component; state is data owned and managed inside a component that can change over time and triggers a re-render when updated.

fields.Front: How do you code a component that increments a counter on button click using useState?
fields.Back:
function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  return (
    <button onClick={() => setCount(c => c + 1)}>
      {count}
    </button>
  );
}

fields.Front: What does the dependency array argument to useEffect control?
fields.Back: When the effect re-runs: an empty array [] runs it once on mount; omitting the array runs it after every render; listing values re-runs it whenever any of those values change.

fields.Front: How do you code a useEffect that subscribes to a window resize event and cleans up on unmount?
fields.Back:
useEffect(() => {
  const onResize = () => setWidth(window.innerWidth);
  window.addEventListener('resize', onResize);
  return () => window.removeEventListener('resize', onResize);
}, []);

fields.Front: What common bug happens when a useEffect reads a state variable but omits it from the dependency array?
fields.Back: A 'stale closure': the effect keeps using the value from the render it was created in, so it never sees later updates to that variable until something else forces a re-run.
It memoizes the result of an expensive computation, recomputing it only when its dependencies change, avoiding unnecessary recalculation on every render.
It memoizes a function reference itself so it isn't recreated on every render, preventing unnecessary re-renders of child components that receive it as a prop (e.g. with React.memo).

fields.Front: What is the virtual DOM in React?
fields.Back: An in-memory, lightweight representation of the real DOM tree that React updates first; React then diffs it against the previous version (reconciliation) to compute the minimal set of real DOM mutations needed.

fields.Front: Why does React require a stable, unique key prop when rendering a list of elements?
fields.Back: Keys let React's reconciler match array items between renders so it can detect insertions, removals, and reorders correctly instead of mismatching or needlessly re-creating DOM nodes.

fields.Front: What's a common pitfall of using the array index as a React list key?
fields.Back: If the list is reordered, filtered, or items are inserted/removed, indices shift and no longer identify the same item, causing React to reuse DOM nodes/state for the wrong items.

fields.Front: How do you code a controlled text input in React?
fields.Back:
function NameInput() {
  const [value, setValue] = useState('');
  return (
    <input
      value={value}
      onChange={e => setValue(e.target.value)}
    />
  );
}

fields.Front: What makes an input 'controlled' vs 'uncontrolled' in React?
fields.Back: A controlled input's value is driven by React state via the value prop and updated through onChange; an uncontrolled input manages its own value in the DOM and is read via a ref.

fields.Front: What is 'lifting state up' in React?
fields.Back: Moving shared state from child components to their closest common ancestor so multiple sibling components can read and update the same data via props.

fields.Front: How do you code sharing a value with deeply nested components without prop drilling, using Context?
fields.Back:
const ThemeContext = createContext('light');

function App() {
  return (
    <ThemeContext.Provider value="dark">
      <Toolbar />
    </ThemeContext.Provider>
  );
}

function Toolbar() {
  const theme = useContext(ThemeContext);
  return <div>{theme}</div>;
}
